title: The 'Stab in the Back' Myth: Blaming Defeat on Others
hero_object: German General Staff Strategic Retreat Map (Western Front, Autumn 1918)
hook: They lost the war. Then came a story blaming someone else.
punchline: A scapegoat can explain away a failure. It can’t change the facts.
visual_paradigm: WWI General Staff Cartography & Imperial Telegrams (Prussian Slate #1E293B, Field Olive #365314, Carmine Red #DC2626)

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: They lost the war. Then came a story blaming someone else.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: In November nineteen-eighteen, Germany surrendered in World War One. Its armies were retreating, allies had collapsed, and frontlines were out of reserves.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: General Ludendorff had told the Kaiser two months earlier that military victory was impossible. But after the armistice, he and other generals invented an excuse.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: The Dolchstoßlegende: the stab-in-the-back myth. They claimed the army was undefeated in the field and betrayed only by traitors, socialists, and Jewish citizens at home.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: It was completely false. Nearly one hundred thousand Jewish Germans served bravely in the German army, and twelve thousand died for their country.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: The generals invented a myth to protect their military reputations, with catastrophic consequences for European history.
scenes.on_screen: GENERALS INVENTED A MYTH TO PROTECT PRIDE

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: A scapegoat can explain away a failure. It can’t change the facts.
scenes.source: Beyond the Myth · Facts, not scapegoats
